title: Trip Time Buffer Calculator: Pad Any Estimate
description: Add a percentage buffer to a travel-time estimate with the Trip Time Buffer Calculator — padded totals and leave-by times. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a 3-hour estimate with a 25% buffer becomes 3 hours 45 minutes — and a 10:00 arrival stops depending on the road's good mood.
quick_answer: The Trip Time Buffer Calculator adds a percentage allowance to a base travel-time estimate and returns the padded total. Enter the estimate from your routing tool and the buffer your experience demands, and read the honest planning figure — the one leave-by times and promises should be built from.

Some arrivals punish lateness with a missed day. Their buffers are not pessimism; they are the price of the plane.
Promise the padded figure, deliver at the unpadded one, and be early more often than explained.
Track estimate versus actual for a month: the ratio is your personal buffer, measured. Most people meet their number with horror and then relief.
3 h × 1.25 = 3 h 45 min. Arrive-by 10:00 → leave 06:15, not 07:00. The 45 minutes is where the traffic jam, the petrol stop and the forgotten passport live.
2 h 30 min × 1.20 = 3 h 00 min exactly. A 20% buffer on a familiar route is often the difference between a plan and a hope.

faq: What does this tool calculate?
A padded travel time: base estimate × (1 + buffer percentage), with the buffer minutes shown as their own figure.
Do I need an account?
No. Estimate and percentage in, padded time out.
Can I rely on this for professional work?
Buffers are how professionals quote — dispatch and logistics run on padded figures. This calculator makes the padding explicit and consistent.
Does the route include live traffic?
No — the buffer is precisely your allowance for the traffic and life the estimate cannot see.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
It inflates the base estimate, which the buffer then scales. Pad the road-based figure, always.
What buffer should I use?
Familiar route, slack deadline: 10–15%. Unfamiliar or high-stakes: 25–50%. Your own estimate-versus-actual history outranks these defaults.
Is a buffer just pessimism?
It is insurance priced in minutes. The unpadded estimate is the journey where nothing unexpected happens — a journey type rarely sighted.
Buffer or earlier alarm — same thing?
The buffer is a property of the plan; the alarm obeys it. Compute the buffer, then set the alarm from the padded figure.
My estimates are always short by half an hour flat.
Then a flat allowance may fit your life better — but check whether the shortfall grows on long trips; percentages win when it does.
Do professionals really add 25%?
Many add more on unfamiliar ground. The visible buffer's virtue is that it can be argued with — the invisible one cannot.
